Ovarian damage from cyclophosphamide

In a cyclophosphamide-treated mouse model, PBM increased ovarian weight and progesterone, reduced follicular apoptosis, and restored vascular markers. The study did not measure preserved fertility or human outcomes (Oubiña et al. 2021).

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a cyclophosphamide-treated mouse model, PBM increased ovarian weight and progesterone, reduced follicular apoptosis, and restored vascular markers. The study did not measure preserved fertility or human outcomes (Oubiña et al. 2021).

Summary of the Evidence

One controlled preclinical publication directly examined cyclophosphamide-induced ovarian injury in mice. It is a single experiment rather than a replicated research programme, and no duplicate report or human trial was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No human study was identified that used PBM to preserve ovarian function during cyclophosphamide treatment. The evidence therefore provides no patient data on menstrual recovery, ovarian reserve, pregnancy, live birth, or safety alongside cancer therapy.

Animal evidence

In mice given cyclophosphamide, local low-level laser treatment increased ovarian weight, serum progesterone, and P450scc protein compared with cyclophosphamide alone. It reduced apoptosis in antral follicles and lowered the BAX-to-BCL-2 ratio. Measures of ovarian vascular structure also returned toward the pattern seen in untreated tissue. These are favorable tissue and hormone changes in the tested model, but they do not show that fertility was preserved (Oubiña et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mouse study used 606-nm visible orange-red light applied locally to the ovaries, with reported fluences of 64, 96, or 128 J/cm² and corresponding exposure times of 80, 120, or 160 seconds. These exposures describe that specific model. No comparison tested a different wavelength or schedule, and the experiment cannot establish a safe human dose or timing relative to chemotherapy (Oubiña et al. 2021).

Interpretation

The observed increases in ovarian weight, progesterone, and vascular markers, together with lower follicular apoptosis, support tissue protection within this mouse model. Whether those changes preserve ovulation and the ability to have healthy offspring remains unknown. Because the proposed setting involves cancer treatment, future work also needs to test whether PBM affects tumour response or chemotherapy effectiveness before clinical use is considered.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for ovarian tissue protection after cyclophosphamide in mice (Oubiña et al. 2021)

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One controlled mouse study found higher ovarian weight and progesterone, less follicular apoptosis, and restored vascular markers after PBM. These outcomes show tissue-level protection in that model, but not preserved ovulation, pregnancy, or offspring health. Independent animal replication with fertility and cancer-treatment safety outcomes would be needed before testing this approach in patients (Oubiña et al. 2021).
